subject: moving-continents
title: Plate Tectonics: How a Paradigm Flipped
summary: Evidence vs. mechanism, the sea-floor data, and what is still unresolved.

keys.prompt: Why was rejecting Wegener in the 1920s defensible?
keys.answer: His evidence was suggestive but his mechanism (continents plowing through oceanic crust) was physically implausible.

keys.prompt: Which predictions of seafloor spreading held?
keys.answer: Youngest rocks at the ridge crest and older with distance, present-day polarity at the crest, symmetric stripes; 1968 drill cores clinched it.

keys.prompt: What is still open in plate tectonics?

cards.title: Evidence without mechanism
cards.text: Wegener's 1912 continental drift had real evidence and was still largely dismissed for decades. Was the field being stubborn, or rational?

cards.question: Plate tectonics is settled science. Is what drives the plates also settled?

options.text: Yes, mantle convection was proven in 1968

cards.reveal: No. USGS notes the driving forces, the very question Wegener couldn't answer, are still debated. The field accepted the pattern before the full mechanism.

cards.title: Why rejection was defensible
cards.text: Wegener's data (coastline fit, matching fossils, coal in Antarctica, glacial deposits in now-arid Africa) were suggestive. But his mechanism, continents plowing through oceanic crust, was physically implausible, as Harold Jeffreys argued. Science weighs an idea's explanatory "how" heavily, and this one failed.

cards.title: New instruments, new data
cards.text: Echo-sounding after World War I showed a rugged sea floor. In 1947 the research ship Atlantis found the Atlantic's sediment far thinner than expected for an ocean billions of years old. By the 1950s, surveys revealed a global mid-ocean ridge more than 50,000 km long.
cards.example: Magnetometers adapted from WWII submarine detection then revealed zebra-like magnetic striping on the sea floor.

why.q: Why was thin Atlantic sediment a clue?
why.a: An ocean floor billions of years old should have collected thick sediment. Thin sediment suggested the floor was much younger.

cards.title: The prediction that held
cards.text: Seafloor spreading predicted that rocks would be youngest at the ridge crest and older with distance, that the youngest would have present-day polarity, and that stripes would be symmetric. All three held. In 1968, Glomar Challenger drill cores dated by fossils and isotopes clinched it.

cards.title: Rates, and an open question
cards.text: Spreading rates range from under 2.5 cm per year (Arctic Ridge) to over 15 cm per year (East Pacific Rise). The San Andreas slips about 5 cm per year on average. Yet USGS notes that what drives the plates, the very question Wegener could not answer, is still debated.

cards.prompt: Rejecting drift for lack of a mechanism, then accepting it after the predictions held: defensible caution or belief perseverance?
cards.model: Mostly defensible: the field updated when risky predictions held. Belief perseverance is holding on after the evidence is discredited, which is not what happened.

cards.question: A field rejected a correct conclusion for decades because the proposed mechanism was wrong. In investing or operations, when should you act on a pattern you can't yet explain?
nudges: What is the cost of being early and wrong vs. late and right?
What evidence would make a mechanism unnecessary for a decision?

questions.q: Which finding most directly supported seafloor spreading?

options.text: Symmetric magnetic stripes, with the youngest rock at the ridge crest
options.why: Yes. It matched the hypothesis's specific predictions.

options.text: The fit of South America and Africa
options.why: That supported drift, but it was Wegener's older evidence and did not show a mechanism.
Climate evidence for drift, not for spreading.
Explained by plate collision, but not the key spreading evidence.

options.text: Solid continents could not plow through oceanic crust without breaking up.
options.why: Right, and he was correct about that mechanism.

options.text: Fossils could have floated across the ocean.
options.why: Wegener argued the organisms could not have crossed. Jeffreys's objection was physical.
The expanding-Earth idea came up later and lacked a mechanism too.
Stripes were found later. Jeffreys argued about mechanics.

questions.q: Per USGS, which question remains debated?

options.text: The nature of the forces that drive the plates

options.why: Settled by drill-core dating by 1968 and later work.
